articles.title: ‘There’s no way’: Jasontheween breaks down after losing 11 hours of GTA 6 progress
articles.summary: Twitch streamer Jasontheween had a terrible experience during his GTA 6 marathon after accidentally turning off his PS5 and losing more than 11 hours of
articles.body: Twitch streamer Jasontheween had a terrible experience during his GTA 6 marathon after accidentally turning off his PS5 and losing more than 11 hours of gameplay. The CORE Boys member was streaming from a rented Airbnb in Miami with his friends when the incident happened. His reaction was caught on stream as he struggled to believe that his progress was gone. Things became even more stressful when police reportedly arrived at the property shortly after the incident, raising claims that the streamer had been targeted in a swatting incident.Jasontheween Accidentally Turns Off PS5 and Loses 11 Hours of GTA 6 ProgressJasontheween had been playing GTA 6 for around 11 hours when his stream suddenly went offline. He later returned using his phone and explained what had happened. At first, he thought his PC was responsible for the problem. However, further details shared after the incident pointed to his foot accidentally switching off an extension cord connected to his PS5.The console shut down before his progress could be saved. When Jason opened GTA 6 again, he expected to continue from where he had stopped. Instead, the game's opening credits appeared, followed by the prologue. That was when he realised he might have lost his entire gaming session.His reaction quickly turned into frustration. He could not believe that he had to start from the beginning after spending so many hours playing. Jason said:"Nah, bro. Nah, I'm not doing this. I swear to god, I'm not doing this. There's no way, right? There's no f***** way! What the f***?!"The streamer was so frustrated that he even ripped off his shirt. His CORE Boys teammate Marlon then walked into the room to check on him.When Marlon asked if he was serious about losing his progress, Jason explained that he had spent more than 11 hours playing the game. He also pointed out that he had woken up at 5 a.m. for the marathon.The streamer later turned to X and tagged Rockstar Games, Sony and PlayStation. He asked whether there was any way to recover his lost progress. In his post, Jason wrote:"I accidentally turned off my PS5 and lost 11 hrs+ of gameplay. Is there any way I can recover my progress? Please I'll do anything."The Economic Times reported on his request for help. However, there was no confirmed recovery of his lost progress in the available reports.Jasontheween's Miami Airbnb Reportedly Targeted in Swatting Incident After GTA 6 MarathonJason's problems did not end with his lost GTA 6 progress. While he was still upset about the incident, police reportedly arrived at the Miami Airbnb where he and other CORE Boys members were staying.The situation raised concerns about a possible swatting incident. During the stream, Jason could be heard saying that police were outside and asking him to come out. He then moved away from the camera to deal with the situation.Swatting involves someone making a false emergency report to bring police to another person's home or location. Streamers can become targets because their locations may be exposed while they are broadcasting live.However, it is important to note that there has been no official confirmation that the police visit was caused by a false emergency call. The claim that Jason was swatted has mainly come from clips and posts shared online.The streamer also had another problem to deal with after losing his game progress. He had to consider starting his GTA 6 journey again rather than continuing from the point he had reached before the PS5 shut down.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A wealthy Canadian businessman transferred more than $30 million to the woman hired to care for his ill wife; after his death, a November 12 appeals court ordered a new trial to decide whether the transfers were gifts
articles.summary: A wealthy Canadian businessman transferred more than $30 million to the woman hired to care for his ill wife, and after his death the question of whether
articles.body: A wealthy Canadian businessman transferred more than $30 million to the woman hired to care for his ill wife, and after his death the question of whether those transfers were gifts has become the centre of a major estate dispute. On November 12, the Ontario Court of Appeal ordered a new trial in Waters Estate v. Henry, finding that the original judge made errors in how he treated the evidence and the legal burden, according to Blaneys Appeals and Law360 Canada.The case involves a man who hired a personal support worker for his housebound wife in 2009. Within weeks, he began transferring large sums to her, and over the next decade he moved more than $30 million across at least 393 transfers. The Court of Appeal has now sent the matter back for a fresh trial to determine whether the money was intended as a gift or was held in trust for the estate.What the transfers involvedBetween 2009 and December 2019, the businessman transferred more than $30 million to the caregiver in at least 393 transactions. About $19 million went toward buying and renovating properties, while much of the rest funded cars, trips, jewellery, and other personal spending.Some of the money belonged to the businessman’s wife, which he controlled under a power of attorney. The estate argued that most of the transfers were investments subject to a resulting trust, while the caregiver claimed they were gifts within a secret intimate relationship.The trial judge had found that the caregiver rebutted the presumption of resulting trust for almost all of the transfers. That finding is now under review after the Court of Appeal identified problems with how the evidence and legal burden were handled.Why the Court of Appeal intervenedThe Court of Appeal held that the trial judge effectively reversed the onus by looking for evidence that the deceased intended to keep an interest in the transfers. Under the law of resulting trusts, the burden is on the person claiming the money was a gift to show that the deceased intended to give it away.The court also found that the trial judge wrongly excluded the deceased’s handwritten notes as hearsay. The court said those notes could show an implied assertion that the deceased was tracking his investments, which could be relevant to whether the transfers were gifts.In addition, the court held that the intimate relationship between the deceased and the caregiver was context, not the independent corroboration required under section 13 of the Evidence Act. This distinction matters because the caregiver’s claim that the transfers were gifts rests partly on the nature of their relationship.What the new trial will decideThe new trial will focus on whether the more than $30 million in transfers were gifts or were held on resulting trust for the estate. The court will need to examine the evidence again with the correct legal framework in place.The Court of Appeal did uphold one part of the original decision. It found that the deceased kept an 80 percent interest in a horse farm business known as King of Hearts, and it upheld the order that the caregiver repay $1,938,000 of the wife’s money.That means the new trial will not revisit every issue from the original case. It will focus on the transfers and whether they were gifts, while the horse farm finding and the repayment order remain in place.What the case showsThe case is an example of how messy these disputes can become when large sums of money are involved and the person who made the transfers is no longer alive to explain his intentions. The estate argues that the money was invested, while the caregiver argues it was given freely.The legal framework matters because a resulting trust presumes that the person who transferred the money retained an interest unless the recipient can prove otherwise. That presumption is what the Court of Appeal says the trial judge failed to apply correctly.The case also shows how evidence such as handwritten notes can become important. The court found that the deceased’s notes could shed light on whether he was tracking investments, which could support the estate’s position that the transfers were not gifts.What happens next?The new trial will allow both sides to present their case and evidence again. The estate will need to show that the transfers were not gifts, while the caregiver will need to prove that they were.The Court of Appeal’s decision does not settle the question of who owns the money. It simply means that the original trial judge’s findings on that issue cannot stand, and the matter must be decided again.For the family, the case is about recovering money they believe belongs to the estate. For the caregiver, it is about defending transfers she says were gifts. The new trial will determine which version of events the court accepts.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: We cut tax, but where are the hires, salary hikes: PM Modi to industry
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a stinging rebuke, PM Modi on Thursday admonished the corporate sector for not passing on the benefit of reduced corporate tax to employees
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a stinging rebuke, PM Modi on Thursday admonished the corporate sector for not passing on the benefit of reduced corporate tax to employees through higher wages or through more hiring because of their greed.New Delhi: In a stinging rebuke, PM Modi on Thursday admonished the corporate sector for not passing on the benefit of reduced corporate tax to employees through higher wages or through more hiring because of their greed."In 2014, the basic corporate tax rate was 30%. We reduced it to 22%. Today, there is no income tax on earnings up to Rs 12 lakh in India. I know you will not clap, because however much one gives, your appetite never seems to be satisfied. I have exempted income up to Rs 12 lakh from tax. Did you increase the salaries of your employees? Did you increase the number of employees? No. The attitude remains: 'Modiji, you do it, we will see'," PM said at the Ficci AGM. He said tax relief to individuals had helped boost consumption and govt had reduced GST rates and speeded up I-T refunds, freeing up money that was earlier stuck for months. The comments came amid fresh demands for tax sops in the upcoming budget with business leaders submitting their wish list to the FM.Businesses are citing cost pressure and weakening demand amid signs of a pick-up in investment.While PM Narendra Modi cited India's rapid growth, he also called upon industry captains to suggest more reform proposals. "I have come because I respect you. But your experience with previous govts has been so bitter that I am paying the price for it. This is not that old govt. This is a friendly govt... Without hesitation and without inhibition, write to me openly and tell me what reforms are still needed."While urging industry to think beyond the domestic market and produce quality products, he asked them "seize the opportunity" offered by the trade agreements that are being signed.At the same time, he reiterated his message to promote 'swadeshi', citing the call made by Mahatma Gandhi in 1930, and flagged pharma, steel and aluminium among sectors for a domestic manufacturing push."Everyone is sitting here and knows this. India is known as the 'pharmacy of the world'. Yet, despite this, India imports APIs, bulk drugs, and drug intermediates worth billions of dollars every year. There are hundreds of such categories where we still depend on imports. Our pharmaceutical industry must understand which ingredients can be produced within India... We already have strength in finished medicines. Now we must also build capability in ingredients." He also called upon industry to step up investment in agriculture.Besides, he suggested that companies look beyond their comfort zone and enter areas that are strategic."Industry must also prepare for the demands that will emerge in the future at both the national and global levels. We must work on those capabilities that, in this era of weaponisation of resources, become all of our responsibility to secure the nation's future. Therefore, my request to you is this: in every long-term investment decision over the next 20 years, make 'India First' your foundation. This will make the country self-reliant and will also open new opportunities for the growth of your businesses."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: An online sneaker marketplace faced FTC allegations over denied refunds for fake or misdescribed shoes and delayed deliveries; the regulator is now sending payments to more than 6,200 customers over shipping delays
articles.summary: Online sneaker marketplace GOAT promised buyers protection if their shoes proved inauthentic or not as described, but the Federal Trade Commission alleges
articles.body: Online sneaker marketplace GOAT promised buyers protection if their shoes proved inauthentic or not as described, but the Federal Trade Commission alleges it denied some of them full refunds. According to the FTC, the company often offered only partial refunds or store credit, and consumers had to keep complaining to obtain relief. GOAT settled the lawsuit. As a result, the FTC said in October 2026 that it is sending 6,205 payments, totalling more than $100,000, to eligible people who paid for expedited shipping between 2020 and 2024. The payments relate to the shipping allegations, not to the Buyer Protection claims.FTC targets GOAT over denied refunds for fake or misrepresented shoesThe FTC alleges that, despite GOAT's "Assurance of Authenticity" and "Buyer Protection Policy", the company misrepresented that it would give full refunds to buyers who asked to return deficient products. The press release lists these as products that were inauthentic, incorrect or otherwise not as described. According to the FTC, GOAT rejected many such return requests outright and provided only partial refunds or in-store credit.GOAT made it difficult for consumers to complain about deficient products. Its customer service practices, the FTC alleges, were designed to give full refunds only to consumers who kept complaining and escalated their return requests. Samuel Levine, then Director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said that forcing consumers to jump through hoops or keep complaining to receive a promised refund is unacceptable under the law.GOAT faces FTC action over delayed orders and shipping refundsThe FTC's complaint also concerns GOAT's shipping promises. The press release says GOAT advertised that "Standard" orders would typically arrive within three to six business days, and that "Next Day" orders usually arrive within one to two days of ordering. The FTC alleges that GOAT shipped 37% of all "Instant" orders later than it promised, and shipped more than 16% of all "Next Day" orders on the second day or later. Buyers had paid between $14.50 and $25 in shipping upgrade charges. In such cases, the FTC alleges, GOAT did not offer buyers the choice of agreeing to the delay or cancelling for a prompt refund, as the Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule requires.Under the proposed court order settling the complaint, GOAT was to pay $2,013,527 in refunds to consumers harmed by its shipping practices. The order would also prohibit the practices described in the complaint, including misrepresenting the relief offered to consumers who receive a deficient product. It would additionally bar GOAT from denying refund or credit requests for specially protected products, including used or final-sale items or requests made late, unless it clearly discloses its denial policies. The Commission vote authorising the complaint and stipulated final order was 5-0, and the documents were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California.FTC sends 6,205 refund payments to GOAT customersAn FTC refund page dated October 2026 states that the agency is sending 6,205 payments, totalling more than $100,000, to eligible people who paid GOAT for expedited shipping between 2020 and 2024. These payments relate to the shipping allegations, not to the Buyer Protection claims. The page says GOAT agreed to settle the lawsuit and, as a result, issued refunds in 2025 that returned more than $736,000 to eligible customers. The FTC is now paying eligible customers who did not receive a refund from GOAT.The FTC says recipients of a cheque should cash it within 90 days, and recipients of a PayPal payment should accept it within 30 days. Questions can be directed to the refund administrator and the FTC also points to a refund payments FAQ page. The 2024 press release notes that the Commission files a complaint when it has "reason to believe" a law is being or is about to be violated, so the conduct described above remains the FTC's allegations.You use AI every day. articles.title: A mother moved her three children from Indiana to California after her husband pleaded guilty to domestic battery; when she refused to return them, she faced 90 days in jail until a November 17 appeals reversal
articles.summary: Navigating family court orders becomes perilous when a single courthouse issues directives that pull a parent in opposite directions.
articles.body: Navigating family court orders becomes perilous when a single courthouse issues directives that pull a parent in opposite directions. For Rajpal Kaur, a mother who relocated with her three children from Indiana to California following her husband’s criminal domestic battery conviction, an interstate divorce dispute escalated into a contempt ruling carrying a 90-day jail sentence and an arrest warrant, before the Indiana Court of Appeals stepped in to reverse the sanction.Contradictory court directives spark contempt sanctionsAccording to records reviewed by the Indiana Court of Appeals, the legal tangle began after Gurminder Singh filed to dissolve his January 2014 marriage to Kaur in Johnson County, Indiana, in September 2025. Following a provisional hearing in October 2025, where Kaur appeared remotely without legal representation, the Johnson Circuit Court issued a provisional order directing her to return the three children to Indiana.However, less than a week later, the very same trial court granted protection orders on behalf of Kaur and the children against Singh. Those protective decrees explicitly restrained Singh from having any contact with the protected family members while noting they were not intended to interfere with valid visitation orders from other courts, the Indiana Court of Appeals noted. When Kaur remained in California with the children rather than returning them, Singh petitioned the court to hold her in contempt. In February 2026, the trial court found Kaur in indirect contempt, sentenced her to 90 days in jail, issued a body attachment for her arrest, and ordered her to pay $6,000 in attorney fees, even though the judge acknowledged during a hearing that the court’s own orders gave contradictory instructions to the parents.Background of relocation and interstate jurisdictionThe family’s cross-country separation stemmed from events in March 2024, when Indiana prosecutors charged Singh with Level 6 felony domestic battery for battering Kaur, according to the Indiana Court of Appeals. Singh pleaded guilty to the offense and received a one-year probation sentence, while Kaur relocated to California with their three children and Singh stayed in Johnson County.Once represented by legal counsel, Kaur moved to set aside the October 2025 provisional custody order, pointing out that she had never been formally served with the divorce summons or hearing notice and challenging the Indiana court’s subject matter jurisdiction under the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction Act, or UCCJA. Although the trial court acknowledged there was no record of proper service, it initially ruled she had waived that objection by participating remotely in the provisional hearing, while scheduling an evidentiary hearing on the interstate jurisdiction issue. By October 2026, the trial court ultimately vacated the underlying provisional order, rendering Kaur’s direct challenge to that order moot on appeal, the Indiana Court of Appeals explained.Appellate panel reverses contempt rulingWhile dismissing the moot jurisdictional claims, the Indiana Court of Appeals emphasized that trial judges bear an affirmative obligation to examine subject matter jurisdiction immediately upon recognizing an interstate custody dispute, adding that procedural irregularities and due process lapses meant Kaur had not waived her UCCJA protections.Turning to the stayed contempt sanctions, the Indiana Court of Appeals ruled that the trial court abused its discretion. Because civil contempt requires willful disobedience of a clear and certain mandate, Kaur could not lawfully be punished for violating a provisional relocation order that directly clashed with protection orders barring her husband from contacting the children, and which the trial court itself had subsequently vacated. Consequently, the appellate panel reversed the contempt finding and eliminated the 90-day jail threat, though it noted Kaur had waived any appellate challenge to the $6,000 attorney fee award.You use AI every day. articles.title: El Niño strikes again, breaking rain records in San Francisco and along Florida’s Atlantic coast
articles.summary: A strong El Nino is once again rearing its head, with storms breaking rainfall records and causing coastal flooding in both California and Florida.
articles.body: As storms pound both coasts on Wednesday and Thursday, a strong El Niño is once again rearing its head, breaking rainfall records and causing coastal flooding in California and Florida. Downtown San Francisco set a new record for daily rainfall Wednesday, at 2.64 inches. The previous record was 2.24 inches on Nov. 18, 1918. “Yesterday completely smashed those records,” said Anamaria Navarette, a National Weather Service meteorologist in the agency’s San Francisco Bay Area office. “El Niño certainly is playing a part in the event.” Two waterspouts — a rotating, tornado-like column of moisture over the sea — formed in the San Francisco Bay on Wednesday, and another near Santa Cruz, to the south. Gusty winds downed trees and power lines, while rain soaked burn scars from past wildfires, prompting flash flood warnings. Meanwhile, on Florida’s Atlantic coast, more than a foot of rain has fallen over the past 48 hours, hitting the same areas that got hammered with historic rainfall just two weeks ago. The prior round of flooding forced ballot boxes to be relocated on Election Day. Melissa Watson, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Melbourne, Florida, described the last two days in much the same way her San Francisco colleague did: “Quite a few records were broken yesterday,” she said when reached by phone, as alert noises blared in the background. “We are in that strong El Niño pattern.” Because the storms earlier this month left much of Florida’s Space Coast soggy, the new round of rain sent the region’s flash flood risk rating to its highest category on Thursday. “It’s not seeping into the earth at all because the soils are completely saturated,” Watson said of the rainwater. The severe storms on both coasts are thought to be linked to El Niño because the climate pattern intensifies Pacific storms that can hit the West Coast and at the same time rejiggers the southern jet stream to direct more storms toward the Southeast. Data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration suggests that this season’s El Niño event was the second-biggest on record for the months of August through October, even when ignoring the influence of climate change. NOAA expects the trend to persist through May. El Niño is a natural pattern that happens when winds near the equator weaken and less cold water rises to the surface in the eastern Pacific Ocean. The pattern drives up global temperatures. In California, the majority of fall and winter precipitation regardless of El Niño is driven by atmospheric river storms: narrow plumes of moisture from the tropical or subtropical Pacific. These storms are responsible for more than $1.1 billion in yearly flood damage, on average, according to a 2022 study. About 84% of flood damage in Western states is associated with atmospheric rivers, research suggests. Although atmospheric rivers are not necessarily more frequent in California during El Niño years, they can pack a stiffer punch because the warm Pacific water provides more fuel to storms. Off the coast of Monterrey, California, sea surface temperatures were about 12 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than average, Navarette said. “A lot of the moisture that we were seeing surging on through yesterday was definitely amplified by those warm ocean temperatures,” she said. In the Southeast and Gulf Coast, El Niño typically lowers temperatures, but it draws storm tracks farther south. Daytona Beach saw nearly 5.8 inches of rain on Wednesday, breaking its previous daily rainfall record by more than 5 inches, Watson said. Some 11 million Floridians were under a flood watch Thursday morning. Melbourne officials opened an emergency shelter at a community center. Gov. Ron DeSantis deployed hundreds of National and State Guard personnel, highway patrollers and wildlife officers to respond to the flooding. On Thursday, rainfall rates were forecast to get as high as 4 inches per hour in parts of Florida. By Saturday, forecasters expect 4 to 8 inches of rain along the coast, with 12 to 15 inches possible in some localized areas. More flooding is likely.

articles.title: "Come up with other games": GTA VI faces fresh backlash as Asmongold calls its storyline a ‘female fantasy’
articles.summary: GTA VI has barely reached players, but it is already attracting strong opinions from some of gaming's biggest online personalities.
articles.body: GTA VI has barely reached players, but it is already attracting strong opinions from some of gaming's biggest online personalities. Twitch and Kick streamer Asmongold has sparked debate over Rockstar Games' latest release after questioning the way its male lead, Jason Duval, is written. His comments about the game's story and character dynamics quickly caught attention. However, his criticism came with an unexpected twist. Despite calling parts of the story a female fantasy, Asmongold admitted he was enjoying the game and gave it an impressive nine out of ten.Asmongold calls GTA VI a female fantasy and questions Jason Duval's characterDuring a livestream on November 18, Asmongold discussed the reactions surrounding GTA VI on social media. The streamer noticed that the game's character writing had become a talking point among players and decided to share his own interpretation.His biggest criticism centred on Jason Duval, one of the game's two main protagonists. Asmongold described Jason as a conventional boyfriend figure who lacks the personality and appeal he would expect from a leading character. He also suggested that the story appeared to reflect a female perspective.Explaining his thoughts, the streamer said:"There are people crashing out about this. I looked at Twitter. People crashing out and having opinions about this. Like, I know that I am goofing around about it a lot. Yeah, I think some of the... I feel like this **** is obviously kinda written by a woman. And, like, you know, Jason is just like your traditional, like, simp, like, boyfriend. Right? He's not really, like, super interesting. It feels kind of like, you know, a female fantasy. Right?"The comments quickly added another layer to the ongoing discussion about GTA VI's storytelling. With Jason and Lucia serving as the central characters, players have been closely examining their relationship and the way Rockstar has chosen to present both protagonists.However, Asmongold made it clear that his remarks should not be mistaken for a dislike of the game."I don't really think it's been bad. I've been enjoying the game. It's been fine. I don't want people to get the wrong idea, like, I hate it or, like, I don't like the game or I don't think it's fun. I'm usually just goofing around with this kind of stuff. I am. I think it's fun."Asmongold rates GTA VI 9/10 despite criticism of its storyInterestingly, Asmongold's overall assessment of GTA VI was far more positive than his comments about Jason might suggest. During the same broadcast, he rated Rockstar's latest release nine out of ten and called it a good game.He did not hold back when discussing the story, though. The streamer described certain narrative elements as "femslop" and repeated his concerns about Jason's character."I would rate it like a nine. I think it's good. No, I'd say it is good. Like, I think some of the story stuff is kind of... I think it's kind of femslop. Right? And Jason isn't like that great of a character. Like, I don't find him to be, like, super interesting or anything. But I don't think the game is, like, bad. Right? 'What game is a 10?' Elden Ring. I could come up with other games that are 10. Right?"His rating suggests that, despite his reservations about the writing, Asmongold sees plenty to enjoy in GTA VI. His comments also add to the growing conversation around Rockstar's character choices as more players experience the highly anticipated release.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Trump clears hurdle in $15 billion lawsuit against New York Times
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s legal team celebrated Thursday after a judge denied The New York Times’ motion to dismiss a $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the paper.
articles.body: President Donald Trump’s legal team is celebrating Thursday after a judge denied The New York Times’ motion to dismiss the president’s $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the paper. U.S. District Judge Steven D. Merryday allowed four counts centered on seven specific accusations of criminal conduct to move forward after Trump’s legal team argued that the Times and publisher Penguin Random House showed reckless disregard, alleging "purposeful avoidance of the truth" in a book authored by Times journalists. "President Trump continues holding the Fake News accountable for deceiving the American people. Judge Merryday has correctly denied the motion to dismiss filed by The New York Times, Penguin Publishing and their writers as to President Trump’s powerhouse defamation lawsuit," a spokesman for Trump’s legal team told Fox News Digital. NEW YORK TIMES LOSES DEFAMATION SUIT, ORDERED TO PAY $9.25M TO FORMER ALABAMA BASKETBALL PLAYER "These defendants will now have to answer for intentionally and maliciously defaming President Trump," the spokesman continued. "The New York Times has a long pattern of defaming President Trump in service of its leftist political agenda, and today’s momentous ruling is a victory for honesty in America." Judge Merryday issued a pointed critique of Susanne Craig and Russ Buettner, the authors of "Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father’s Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success," for publishing definitive claims of complex tax fraud and money laundering without a formal legal opinion or forensic auditing. Merryday observed that accusations were made against Trump and his father without charges or convictions. "In other words, the facts alleged in the complaint create at least a plausible inference that the authors and the publishers knew that no reliable conclusion about violations of the tax laws, including especially the estate and gift tax laws, is possible without reliance on qualified opinion formulated after the necessary factual and legal research and analysis, which they knowingly failed to obtain," Merryday wrote. TRUMP TOUTS LEGAL VICTORY OVER BBC AS JUDGE SAYS HIS LAWSUIT AGAINST BRITISH BROADCASTER CAN PROCEED The court dismissed the Times’ reliance on outside commentators, such as a former prosecutor saying a Trump transaction "smells like a crime" and a professor who called the action "suspicious." "Obviously, even a qualified expert offering a superficial characterization such as a transaction is ‘suspicious’ or ‘could’ violate the law or attributing to a transaction the ‘smell’ of crime or noting that a gift tax return can evade IRS scrutiny or generously giving his immensely valuable time to aid laypersons ‘lost in the weeds’ is far from a formal legal opinion sufficient to remove serious doubt about the truthfulness and accuracy of a statement accusing a specific person of fraud or tax evasion or some related crime arising from a specific transaction," Merryday wrote. While Trump’s lawsuit can move forward, Merryday also dismissed two counts and threw out 27 other challenged statements as non-actionable under the strict First Amendment protections of New York Times Co. v. Sullivan and denied Trump's request to amend his complaint a third time. TRUMP DOJ WITHDRAWS SUBPOENAS TARGETING NEW YORK TIMES JOURNALISTS AMID LEAK PROBE A New York Times spokesperson provided the following statement to Fox News Digital: "The Times is encouraged to see Judge Merryday’s dismissal of almost all claims against us. We continue to believe the remaining claim in the filing has no legal merit. We look forward to making this argument as we continue to defend ourselves against this baseless attack on The Times and the rights of the free and independent press in this country." The judge ordered The New York Times to file a formal answer within 28 days. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital’s Joseph A. Wulfsohn contributed to this report.

articles.title: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of the lunch break
articles.summary: What is acceptable to eat at your desk, without annoying your colleagues?
articles.body:
There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's.

Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish.

From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive.

"We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah.

She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left".

Casey, a content creator for an energy company, says he used to eat tuna at his desk but has since "reformed".

He says you have to "suss out the smelliness" and then decide if it's acceptable to eat at the desk.

But fish isn't the only food causing office friction and Casey says his regular snack of cinnamon pretzels has been causing "quite a bit of havoc".

"The sugar's going everywhere and it's getting in my laptop keys," he admits. No-one in the office has commented on it yet but he says he's hiding the crumbs by "shuffling them off the desk".

Boiled eggs also split opinion. Laura, who works in finance, says she's been teased by colleagues for eating them.

"In my defence, it was high protein, it was cost-effective and healthy – I swear by a good boiled egg."

She thinks that no food is off limits at the desk. "Coming from an Asian background where you'd eat fish for breakfast I am very open to it being eaten."

Ashlea Fisher, who runs her own recruitment company, has tackled the issue of smelly food in the office head on when she asked a member of staff to stop bringing in fish after "the smell was so bad that a pregnant colleague was feeling physically sick".

"I'm a big believer in being able to have an honest conversation with your team," she says, and suggests that other people in her position should approach a conversation lightly and be conscious of not embarrassing colleagues.

"Nobody should feel judged for what they eat, and we should respect different cultures and dietary requirements, but being mindful of the people around you is simply good workplace etiquette."

While what we eat in the office at lunch can cause tension, there's also the question of whether we're even taking the time to enjoy our lunch in the first place.

In a world of back-to-back meetings and overflowing inboxes, it's easy to skip our break and shovel down a sandwich with one hand while replying to emails with the other.

A 2025 report by Just Eat found that the youngest workers, Gen Z, were the most likely to take a full break, with 56% doing so.

However, the next generation up, millennials were more likely than any other to eat lunch at their desk.

"While it can be convenient to eat at your desk, it's not best practice to remain glued to the screen all day," says Alan Price, an employment law and HR expert, and CEO of BrightHR.

"Taking a break isn't just an employment right, there are proven benefits for both physical and mental health."

Laura, whose working day can occasionally finish at 2am, says stepping away from her desk is a non-negotiable and she makes a point of taking an hour for lunch, describing it as "essential for maintaining my sanity".

"I take my lunch break as much as possible, for the sake of my eyes and mental wellbeing," she says.

But others are less precious about it. Content creator Manny says he has lunch at his desk "most of the time".

His work is task-based and his company operates a policy of "do the work when you want to do it".

"Usually you just take 20 minutes to eat something, but on another day you might take an hour. You just kind of feel it out," he says.

articles.title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
articles.summary: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in Taiz by the Houthis who reveal what life is like under siege.
articles.body:
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.

"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."

She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.

"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.

War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.

Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.

A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.

An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.

Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."

Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.

They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.

He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.

"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.

It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.

"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."

He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.

On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.

The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.

That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.

He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".

Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.

"Until the population perishes," he replies.

They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.

They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.

Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.

Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.

Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.

He tells us this fight is different to 2015.

"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."

He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.

But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".

The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.

"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."

But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.

"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."

The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."

Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.

Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.

"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.

His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.

Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.

"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."

As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.

"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."

articles.title: The Hunger Games: Why joining the franchise is 'nerve-racking' for new stars
articles.summary: The prequel, which is set 24 years before the original The Hunger Games film, is released today.
articles.body:
It's been 14 years since the release of the first Hunger Games movie, which helped establish the careers of talented young actors Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler.

This latest instalment, prequel film Sunrise on the Reaping, looks to do the same with its leading trio: 21-year-old Joseph Zada, 20-year-old Mckenna Grace and 23-year-old Whitney Peak.

Sitting down with BBC News at the start of a gruelling press run, the group were buzzing with a mixture of anticipation, nerves and excitement ahead of the release of the much-talked-about film.

Zada, who is taking on his first major role as lead Haymitch Abernathy, said they had been "clinging together" and "using each other, making sure we all feel supported".

'Nothing like anything I've experienced'

Grace is the most experienced of the three, having grown up as a child star with appearances in TV series The Handmaid's Tale, The Haunting of Hill House and two of the recent Ghostbusters films.

Even then, she said joining The Hunger Games franchise is "so nerve-racking", adding "I don't think anything can prepare you for working on it - this is nothing like anything I've experienced."

Peak, who starred in Netflix's Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, jokes that she and Zada have sought out Grace every time they have felt "stuck or confused about what's happening" while promoting the film, and Zada says she has been a "mentor" to the new actors.

Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth film in the series, which to date is one of the highest-grossing film franchises of all time, bringing in more than $3.3bn (£2.51bn) worldwide since 2012.

It is set 24 years before the original The Hunger Games film and is based on the 2025 book of the same name by author Suzanne Collins.

Zada takes on the role of a teenage Haymitch, who is played by Woody Harrelson in the original films - a District 12 tribute in the games, chosen alongside Grace's character Donner.

Peak plays Lenore Dove, Haymitch's girlfriend.

Reviews of the latest film have been generally positive, with several outlets praising Zada's performance, noting the difficulty of stepping into Harrelson's shoes.

Zada says he spent months "completely invested" in Harrelson's performances in the first four The Hunger Games films, "watching everything I could find and then making notes" which he used "as a base layer to colour with my own ideas".

He didn't meet the Oscar-nominated actor until halfway through filming, but says his advice was to watch two films - Cool Hand Luke and Harold and Maud, with the former "helping a lot to ground my performance" and the latter serving as "a fun watch".

Jesse Plemons, who plays a games producer in the film, told the BBC he knew Zada's role would be "a massive undertaking" after reading the script but says he was "amazed by his stamina and grace".

This was echoed by Glenn Close, who plays an over-the-top representative from the ruling Capitol, who said she "loved working with" Zada.

"When I met them [Zada, Grace and Peak] for the first time, they'd done all the games and been through it all.

"The first thing Joe said to me was 'I'm a bit traumatised' and he wasn't even done - there was still so much to go," she added.

The film, which includes an ensemble cast of Ralph Fiennes, Maya Hawke, Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning, is set during the 50th edition of The Hunger Games - with most elements of the brutal dystopian universe that fans have come to recognise from the previous films returning in this iteration.

Adapted from Collins' novels, the series is set in a post-apocalyptic North America, which is known as Panem, with the first trilogy focusing on a teenage Katniss Everdeen, who was played by Lawrence in the films.

Panem has 12 districts that participate in the yearly Hunger Games, produced and run by the governing area, the Capitol, as a punishment for rebellion.

Peak notes that being on set was an intense experience for the young cast and could "get overwhelming very quickly" on set, so they had to make sure to "keep it light between all the hard stuff".

"I don't think people realise how intensely bonding an experience like this is because we all spend days doing extremely physical and deeply emotional things," Grace says.

"It's like a little family on set; we've all been thankful to have each other," she added.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in cinemas now.

articles.title: Does our ethnicity change how we experience dying?
articles.summary: Death is the one certainty we all share - but could our ethnicity change how we go through it?
articles.body:
We're all going to die - and whether we think about it consciously or not, we generally hope that it will be as smooth as possible for ourselves and our loved ones.

But a study published earlier this year by King's College London and the University of Sheffield suggests that your ethnicity could play a role in how likely this is to be the case.

The research found that people from minority ethnic backgrounds experiencing end-of-life care and grief often struggled to access culturally and religiously appropriate support.

One woman told researchers a hospital sent an Imam - a Muslim religious leader - to her father's bedside when he was dying, even though their family were Hindu.

That lack of culturally appropriate resources or training is exacerbating an "incredibly difficult time in their lives where they were really vulnerable", says Sabrina Bajwah, one of the study's co-authors.

So how can our ethnic or cultural background shape what kind of death we have? And what kind of support is available?

Bajwah told the BBC researchers discovered different types of inequality in their research.

"There was the structural racism that people talked about, which was the 'treating everybody equally' - and by treating everybody equally, services weren't meeting the needs of these communities," she said. "Then there was the other, direct form of racism."

A study last year from the NHS Race and Health Observatory, set up in 2021 to try and tackle racial inequalities within the wider healthcare system, found there was an "alarming" lack of trust among some ethnic minority groups in the care or service they receive.

For example, just over half of participants said they had experienced some form of discrimination from their healthcare providers.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care, which commissioned this year's study, told the BBC that "ethnicity or background should never be a barrier to accessing bereavement support and everyone has the right to the same level of care".

"We will consider the findings of this research project carefully as part of future policy making," they said.

Pravin Navekar's wife Gita started experiencing chronic pain in her back and legs in 2010, but despite multiple GP visits over a two-year period, was repeatedly sent home with pain relief and no further investigations.

In the end the couple, from Leicester, paid to see a consultant privately, at which point Gita was referred for a CT scan. This picked up a rare cancer, a synovial sarcoma, in her pelvis.

Though she was given a prognosis of under five years when she was first diagnosed, Gita lived for another 11, before passing away in April 2021.

Pravin felt culturally appropriate care was "lacking" at times when Gita was in hospital.

"We're all individuals and we have individual needs and wants, and they're tied in with your faith, your culture, your beliefs," he said.

"If she was in hospital for Diwali, then it was another normal day. But when you have Christmas they do all sorts of things and make people really comfortable… [for Diwali] they don't even acknowledge it. There's nothing wrong with a nurse or a doctor coming up to you and saying, 'Good morning, and happy Diwali to you'.

"It's about recognising a person as a whole person, rather than somebody in a bed who needs care."

When Marwa Soliman's father died in 2013, she had just moved from Egypt to Nottingham and was pregnant with her third child. She didn't know anyone, and had struggled to find a community.

"I just remember crumbling on the floor and crying, not knowing what to do and feeling alone and afraid," she said.

Six years later, Marwa set up a support group for Muslim, Arabic-speaking women called Heya - meaning "she" in Arabic.

It's grown from 50 women at the start to more than 700. If there's a death in the community, they all rally around to support each other.

"People send condolences and speak to each other, read the Quran together, we can send out timings if they'd like people to visit," she said.

Marwa has since lost three other close family members, including her mother - but she says having Heya made the experience completely different.

"When the other deaths happened, I had hot food, people coming over, people calling… It's a beautiful thing," she said.

But she worries that other communities won't have the same support, and that funding is scarce for the groups that do exist.

"I think there should be more research, and a clear support and referral path with information about where to go and who to speak to," she said.

Marwa's experience, and the group she set up because of it, could be an example to the Department of Health and Social Care, Catriona Mayland, one of the study's co-authors from Sheffield University, told the BBC.

"Services shouldn't look to replace what's already there," she said. "There's some real strengths within communities that we've seen, and [we should think] actually, how can we build on that and work together?"

articles.title: 'Friend of mine': Trump plays down Musk's MAGA distancing after midterm losses
articles.summary: US president Donald Trump has responded after billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk distanced himself from the Republican president's Make America Great
articles.body: US president Donald Trump has responded after billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk distanced himself from the Republican president's Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, following the party's losses in the midterm elections. Musk, who spent more than $400 million backing Trump-aligned Republican candidates in November, said he felt “pretty foolish” about the money spent and insisted he was not a MAGA supporter.“I mean, I’m not MAGA,” Musk told The New York Times on Wednesday at the DealBook Summit, marking a notable shift in tone from his earlier public association with Trump's political movement.Asked to explain his position, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO said: “I’m not sure what MAGA means.” He added, “But I, I don’t think I’m, like, if, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are, there, there are positives and negatives in both parties.”Trump, speaking to NBC News in a telephone interview on Thursday while returning from his Asia trip, appeared to play down Musk's remarks. “He’s a friend of mine,” the US president said. “What can I tell you? I mean, you have to ask — there are lots of definitions out there.”Trump also said, “MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well.” He added: “But Elon is — Elon’s got very good intentions. I mean, he was with me the whole — he traveled with me.”Musk's comments come after Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections, with Democrats securing victories across several contests. Among the setbacks was the defeat of Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton, whom Musk had backed with around $200 million.Reflecting on his political spending, Musk told DealBook columnist Andrew Sorkin that he would reconsider the amount if given another opportunity.“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” he said. “Or maybe it would’ve been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money.”Musk had been among Trump's most prominent supporters, sitting alongside other technology billionaires at the president's second inauguration on January 20, 2025. He also led the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), becoming one of the administration's most visible figures.The political shift has wider implications for technology companies as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and several state governments in January. Democratic lawmakers have signalled plans for greater scrutiny of artificial intelligence companies, data centre expansion and technology executives' dealings with the Trump administration.Musk is not the only technology leader facing questions over political affiliations. Palantir chief executive Alex Karp recently told Politico, “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment.”Democratic lawmakers, however, appeared unconvinced by Musk's attempt to distance himself from the MAGA movement. Responding to his remarks, Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona wrote on X: “You are still getting a subpoena.” Democrats have indicated that they intend to scrutinise technology companies and their relationships with the Trump administration once they assume control of Congress in January.The prospect of increased scrutiny also extends beyond Musk's political spending. Democratic lawmakers are preparing to examine technology firms' dealings with the Trump administration, their artificial intelligence operations and the rapid expansion of data centres. Separately, Democratic lawmakers in Mississippi have called for an investigation into a reported surge of around 60,000 inactive voter registrations during the midterm elections compared with 2024. The increase was apparently linked to the integration of data from credit reporting agency Experian into the state's voter-roll maintenance process. The issue has drawn attention following Democrat Scott Colom's historic, narrow Senate victory over his Republican opponent.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Rannvijay Singha says being away from his kids for 35 days was tougher than any Roadies challenge; he now tries to squeeze seven workdays into three for family time
articles.summary: For someone who has spent years travelling across cities and countries for TV reality shows, taking on adventure challenges and shooting in different
articles.body: For someone who has spent years travelling across cities and countries for TV reality shows, taking on adventure challenges and shooting in different locations, being away from home is not new. But Rannvijay Singha says his longest separation from his children turned out to be the most difficult experience of his life.In a recent conversation with NDTV, the actor and television host revealed that he had spent 35 to 36 days away from his children, daughter Kainaat and son Jahaanvir. He was speaking during the promotions of his show ‘Roadies REBIRTH’ when he was asked about the toughest task he had faced that year."The most difficult task this year for me was to stay away from my kids for these many days. This is the longest that I've stayed away from them. Including today, I think 35-36 days. I'm going to see them tomorrow. Within 24 hours, I'll be with them. I haven't done anything as hard as this in my life," he told NDTV.Rannvijay is married to Prianka Vohra, and the couple have two children. He said fatherhood has changed how he approaches his professional commitments. Rather than accepting as much work as possible, he now tries to organise his schedule around the time he can spend with his family.“Seven days? No, you have three!”Rannvijay revealed that his decision to reduce work has also made things challenging for his manager and agency. He wants to complete professional commitments in fewer days so that weekends remain available for his children. "My manager is here. She is very young, but losing her hair because of me. Because I am trying to work as little as possible, so that I can stay around my kids," he said.Recalling a conversation with his manager about scheduling, he explained that she would tell him that certain assignments needed one day each and that there were seven days of work to complete. He added that his manager and agency now have to work out how to fit a week's assignments into three days.He did not take a holiday between 2003 and 2012Rannvijay also spoke about how his idea of taking time off has changed since he got married. He recalled that before meeting Prianka, he had not consciously planned a holiday for years, even though his work involved travelling frequently. "Earlier, till I met my wife, I hadn't taken a holiday since I started working. From 2003 to 2012, I hadn't taken a holiday," he said.He explained that his work had taken him to several countries, including Brazil and the US. However, these trips were professional commitments rather than holidays planned for personal time.Today, weekends have become particularly important to him. Since his children do not have school on Saturdays and Sundays, he tries to avoid scheduling work on those days so that he can spend the full day with them.He wants to work less for the next decadeRannvijay said his decision to reduce work is not just a temporary adjustment. He has a longer-term plan to remain active professionally while taking on fewer projects. "For the next nine, ten years, this is what I want to do. I want to work as little as possible, stay relevant. Make sure that instead of doing four shows on MTV now, I only do one," he told NDTV.He also explained why he considers the present years important. As children grow older, their routines and the amount of time they want to spend with their parents change. "I'm hoping this works out for us as a family because once they're 15, they won't need so much of my time. Of course, they'd want me to be around, but not this much. So we'll see. That's the whole idea. Right now, it's changed like that," he said.Rannvijay has been associated with Roadies since its first season in 2003, initially appearing as a contestant before becoming one of the show's best-known hosts.You use AI every day. articles.title: BYD offers full refunds to 1,265 Australian customers who bought cars believing they were 2026 models, only to discover the vehicles were built in 2025
articles.summary: More than 1,200 Australians who purchased electric and hybrid vehicles from BYD discovered that their cars were built in 2025, although they had believed
articles.body: More than 1,200 Australians who purchased electric and hybrid vehicles from BYD discovered that their cars were built in 2025, although they had believed they were buying 2026 models. The company initially offered affected customers $1,100 in compensation, but the amount prompted complaints from buyers who questioned whether it adequately addressed the mistake.The issue came to light after customers contacted the ABC about the vehicles and the proposed payment. According to ABC News, BYD later apologised, blamed the mistake on an administrative error and committed to offering all 1,265 affected customers a full refund.How 2025-built cars were sold to customers expecting 2026 modelsBYD initially contacted affected customers to inform them that their vehicles were 2025 builds instead of the 2026 models they had expected and offered them $1,100 in compensation, which Zoheb Khan said BYD told him was the dealer delivery fee. The company changed its offer after the ABC contacted it for comment. It then committed to providing a full refund to all 1,265 affected customers.BYD public relations director Paul Ellis said, "We will offer customers a full refund. They will take that refund and if they wish to have a new transaction they can purchase another BYD from us."He said the company would contact affected buyers by call, email, and text to explain the updated offer. Customers could also choose to accept the original $1,100 repayment, according to Ellis, under the updated arrangement directly.How the dispute began after BYD customers checked their vehicle detailsThe ABC spoke to four customers in New South Wales, Victoria and Western Australia who described the original compensation as inadequate. Melbourne resident Zoheb Khan said he felt deceived after BYD customer care called to explain that his car had been built in 2025, despite the year stated on his contract.He said, "It's very unethical, seems to be very cheap tactics to me.”He had bought a Premium Atto 3 electric vehicle for $47,000 after rising petrol prices influenced his decision.Khan checked the vehicle identification number, which confirmed the build year. He rejected the $1,100 offer and asked for $3,000 or a replacement vehicle built in 2026.He said, "I don't see any sense of urgency in the company to deal with this."Sydney customer Kirill Kononov also sought a higher payment, a replacement or a full refund before the company changed its position.He said, "I cannot believe that nobody knew about this issue before delivering the cars.”BYD explains the administrative error behind the wrong build datesEllis told the ABC that BYD had mistakenly used the dates on which the vehicles left the factory instead of their manufacturing dates. He described the problem as an administrative error and denied there had been deceit.The company said the vehicles were not materially different, although it acknowledged that the build date was incorrect. Ellis said, "It doesn't affect the compliance of the car in terms of Australian design rules. It doesn't affect the vehicle's warranty or its performance. It is just a build date."He also said customers could buy a new 2026 vehicle for around the amount they had paid previously.Consumer advocate calls for investigation into BYD's vehicle salesErin Turner, CEO of the Consumer Policy Research Centre, questioned whether BYD had misled customers and called for the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission to investigate. She said consumer protections covered situations in which a company promised one thing but supplied another.Turner said, "There are very clear and strong protections against misleading and deceptive behaviour and this could easily fall within that. This law applies when a company promises one thing and doesn't deliver. If you're delivered a 2025 vehicle and you've paid for a 2026, to me that sounds misleading."You use AI every day. Matt Henry and Kyle Jamieson shared the new ball and conceded 16 between them, four of those overs maidens, so India has started carefully rather than quickly.

India trails by 352 with all ten wickets standing and a minimum of 41 overs left in the day.

Day 2, 2nd session: New Zealand all out for 368 as Bumrah finishes with four

India needed only 13 overs after lunch to end the innings, taking the last four wickets for 51 runs after New Zealand had resumed on 317/6.

Jasprit Bumrah finished with 4/92 from 29 overs, and Akash Deep was the pick of the attack with 3/53 from 23, while Anshul Kamboj took 2/69 and Prasidh Krishna 1/100.

Nathan Smith made 14 before Prasidh trapped him lbw, Kyle Jamieson hit 11 and edged Akash Deep to KL Rahul, Matt Henry fell lbw to Bumrah for 1, and Jacob Duffy was caught behind off Kamboj for 4.

Henry Nicholls was left stranded on 175 not out from 335 balls with 21 fours, having batted through 93 overs from the fall of the second wicket.

Day 2, Lunch: NZ 317/6 after Glenn Phillips falls for 118

Shortly after New Zealand brought up their 250, Phillips reached his second Test century off 194 balls. He and Nicholls had come together with the hosts 70/5.

Phillips was bowled by Akash Deep for 118 off 216 balls with 14 fours, ending a sixth-wicket stand of 216 from 394 deliveries.

The hundred was his third against India in 2026, having also made one in an ODI at Indore and one in a T20I at Auckland.

Nicholls went to lunch on 146, with Nathan Smith for company on the 13 after a 31-run stand.

Day 1, Stumps: NZ 243/5. Nicholls and Phillips put on an unbroken 173 for the sixth wicket

What an incredible show from Nicholls and Phillips as they remained unbeaten at the end of the day's play. Nicholls completed his century while Phillips finished on 94, and the hosts will look to turn this into a competitive total on the second morning.

New Zealand bounced back through that sixth-wicket partnership after the early collapse, and it was a frustrating second session for the Indian bowlers.

Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra fell for only 19 runs between them, leaving New Zealand in serious early trouble, but Henry Nicholls steadied the ship with a solid 29 off 58 deliveries, including four boundaries. You sense a strong knock from him today could go a long way towards keeping New Zealand in this contest.

This always felt like a fielding-friendly wicket, and so it has proved in this opening session. Jasprit Bumrah accounted for Tom Latham on the third ball, and the tourists have looked in control from there.

India won the toss and elected to bowl first.

India and New Zealand are set to play the two-match Test series, starting with the first Test at the Basin Reserve ground in Wellington on Thursday.

As Shubman Gill captains India, while Tom Latham leads New Zealand, this will be India's first Test series in New Zealand since the 2019-20 tour, when the hosts secured a 2-0 series sweep with convincing wins in Wellington and Christchurch.

Star spinner Mitchell Santner will miss the series with a fractured right hand, a blow for the home side. India, at least, have Shubman Gill, whose 1,024 runs this cycle are more than anyone in the competition has scored.

articles.title: Army delays controlled detonation of unstable bomb-making chemical in Iowa
articles.summary: The Army postponed the controlled detonation of 68 drums of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, citing a temperature drop.
articles.body: The U. S. Army postponed Friday's planned controlled detonation of five tons of unstable bomb-making chemicals at an Iowa munitions plant until Monday, Nov. 23, amid an incoming temperature drop, environmental lawsuits and a call to delay the blast from Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds. Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle directed Army Materiel Command to push back the operation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, placing the detonation at the latest possible window before the weather shifts. "Public safety is the Army’s top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow’s controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23," Telle said in a statement on X. IOWA RESIDENTS NEAR AMMUNITION PLANT TOLD TO VACATE BEFORE ARMY DETONATES 5 TONS OF BOMB-MAKING CHEMICALS "This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," the statement added. The pause came after Reynolds urged the Army to delay the operation amid growing public safety concerns in the region, while environmental groups filed lawsuits seeking to halt the planned detonation. The decision delays a temporary evacuation for the roughly 400 residents of Middletown, who had been advised to leave their homes Friday morning due to "the potential for localized window damage" and a dust plume containing lead particles. Crews are preparing to detonate 68 drums of degraded lead azide, a chemical used to set off munitions that had been stored in bunkers at the plant for more than 20 years. Army officials discovered in March that water had evaporated from the barrels' stabilizing bath, allowing the material to recrystallize and become too unstable to handle or relocate safely. "The recrystallization of lead azide has created a risk of spontaneous explosion due to the material’s sensitivity to friction and shock, creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation," the Environmental Protection Agency said earlier this month when approving an emergency permit for the blast. CALIFORNIA OFFICIALS WARN MASSIVE CHEMICAL TANK WILL LIKELY SPILL THOUSANDS OF GALLONS OR 'BLOW UP' An Army smoke model released Tuesday projected the plume could reach 25 miles north to Wapello, Iowa, and spread across parts of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois, potentially settling on farmland and playgrounds. The model also noted that "Children under six are especially vulnerable to lead exposure." The Army said it will continue coordinating with the EPA and state and local officials to share updated safety and evacuation guidance ahead of Monday's rescheduled detonation. articles.body: Quinnipiac University was placed on lockdown Thursday evening in response to a reported gunman on campus, according to university officials. "Please stay inside," the university said on social media. "There are reports of a possible gunman on campus." Police are responding to the area. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There is a heavy police presence on campus to deal with this matter," the post said. The alert was also sent through text message to the campus community. A university spokesperson told Fox News Digital that the reported threat prompted a response from local police, but officers have not yet found the suspected gunman. Police continue to investigate.
